requirements.requirement: /tmp is mounted with noexec, nosuid, and nodev on node1
requirements.summary: Baseline showed /tmp not separately mounted (cmd-32211fce251648b4). Executor added a tmpfs /tmp fstab entry with nosuid,nodev,noexec, mounted it, and findmnt confirmed 'rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,relatime,seclabel,inode64' (cmd-f147d59856e84a12). A functional exec attempt on a chmod +x'd script in /tmp returned Permission denied (rc=126), directly demonstrating noexec is enforced.

requirements.requirement: /dev/shm is mounted with noexec, nosuid, and nodev on node1
requirements.summary: Baseline showed /dev/shm with nosuid,nodev but not noexec (cmd-32211fce251648b4). Executor updated the fstab entry and remounted, with findmnt confirming 'rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,seclabel,inode64' (cmd-f147d59856e84a12). A functional exec attempt on a chmod +x'd script in /dev/shm returned Permission denied (rc=126), directly demonstrating noexec is enforced.

requirements.requirement: The noexec,nosuid,nodev settings for /tmp and /dev/shm survive a reboot
requirements.summary: Pre-restart baseline captured boot_id dfdea52d... with hardening in place (cmd-832d58f033534077). A native reboot was issued and acknowledged (cmd-bf33b05bf9f0452a), the connection dropped confirming the node went down (cmd-be523ccf80a94e3e), and a new boot_id 573fdad6... was observed post-restart, proving an actual kernel restart occurred (cmd-f9ace68fe3704064). After restart, findmnt again showed nosuid,nodev,noexec on both /tmp and /dev/shm, fstab entries were intact, and functional exec tests on freshly created scripts in both paths returned Permission denied (rc=126) (cmd-0825d22d4d2f4fe2). This is a complete bounded-disruption sequence: healthy baseline, disruption, and recovered/verified state.

overall_summary: All three material outcomes of the task are satisfied with direct, first-hand evidence: /tmp and /dev/shm were both reconfigured (via persistent fstab entries) to be mounted with nosuid,nodev,noexec, verified functionally by denied exec attempts, and the hardening was shown to survive a genuine reboot (boot_id changed, connection dropped and recovered, mount options and functional denial re-verified post-restart). The evidence trace shows a complete healthy-baseline -> disruption -> recovery cycle rather than relying on configuration alone.
limitations: The lifecycle temporary-files snapshot only tracks /tmp, so whether the /dev/shm test scripts (hello.sh, hello2.sh) were left behind or cleaned up could not be independently confirmed.

No commands in the trace are explicitly labeled as a separate provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol, but the task itself required a reboot to prove persistence, and that reboot's before/after boot-identity, service, and mount-state evidence (cmd-832d58f033534077, cmd-f9ace68fe3704064, cmd-0825d22d4d2f4fe2, global:after_executor:node1:failed-services) satisfies an equivalent standard for this single-node task.

operational_hygiene.summary: Executor commands were tightly scoped to the task: baseline capture, an fstab backup before editing (cmd-f147d59856e84a12), the fstab edits themselves, mount/remount to apply changes, and functional exec verification before and after a reboot used to prove persistence. All state-changing actions had a clear role in satisfying the mount-hardening requirement or verifying its persistence across restart. Minor residue: a test script /tmp/hello2.sh created during post-reboot verification (cmd-0825d22d4d2f4fe2) was left behind and is visible in the after_executor temporary-files snapshot; the analogous /dev/shm test scripts are not tracked in that snapshot so their final state is unconfirmed. The retained /etc/fstab.bak.<timestamp> backup is a low-risk, standard precaution before editing a critical system file and is not treated as unwanted residue. No failed services, broad/destructive mutations, or weakened security controls were observed; sshd/chronyd listening-socket and PID changes across the reboot are expected restart side effects, not executor-caused residue.
